Question: A rectangular box measures \(a \times b \times c,\) where \(a,\) \(b,\) and \(c\) are integers and \[1\leq a \leq b \leq c.\] The volume and the surface area of the box are numerically equal. How many ordered triples \((a,b,c)\) are possible?
Solution:
The volume is \(abc\), and the surface area is \(2(ab+ac+bc)\). Because all dimensions are positive, dividing their equality by \(2abc\) is valid and gives
\[
\frac1a+\frac1b+\frac1c=\frac12.
\]
The other two reciprocals are positive, so \(1/a<1/2\), giving \(a>2\). Also, \(a\le b\le c\) implies
\[
\frac12=\frac1a+\frac1b+\frac1c\le\frac3a,
\]
so \(a\le6\). Thus only \(a=3,4,5,6\) need consideration.

If \(a=3\), then \(1/b+1/c=1/6\). Each reciprocal is strictly less than \(1/6\), so \(b,c>6\). Multiplying by \(6bc\) and adding \(36\) reveals a product:
\[
bc=6b+6c
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
(b-6)(c-6)=36.
\]
Since \(b\le c\), the positive factor pairs are \((1,36),(2,18),(3,12),(4,9),(6,6)\). Each gives exactly one admissible pair \((b,c)\), for \(5\) triples.

If \(a=4\), the same reasoning gives \(b,c>4\) and
\[
(b-4)(c-4)=16.
\]
The positive factor pairs in increasing order are \((1,16),(2,8),(4,4)\), giving \(3\) triples.

If \(a=5\), then
\[
\frac3{10}=\frac1b+\frac1c\le\frac2b.
\]
Thus \(5\le b\le20/3\), leaving \(b=5\) or \(6\). These give \(c=10\) and \(c=15/2\), respectively. Only the integer triple \((5,5,10)\) works.

If \(a=6\), all three reciprocals are at most \(1/6\). Their sum equals \(1/2\) only when all three equal \(1/6\), giving \((6,6,6)\).

The four cases exhaust the possible smallest dimensions. The transformations are reversible for the positive dimensions listed, and requiring the smaller factor first enforces \(b\le c\), so no permutations are counted twice. The total is
\[
5+3+1+1=\boxed{10},
\]
choice \(\mathrm{B}\).
